passage: Suppose a painting has hung for decades in a museum, admired by critics and loved by visitors, and is then shown beyond doubt to be a forgery. Nothing about the canvas has changed: its colours and its composition are exactly as they were, and the pleasure that thousands took in it was genuine pleasure, not a misunderstanding awaiting correction. Yet the picture is taken down, its value collapses, and the critics who praised it are embarrassed. If what matters in a painting is what can be seen in it, this reaction looks irrational, a triumph of the label over the eye.

Two familiar explanations are offered, and neither is adequate. The first says the reaction is mere snobbery: we cared about the famous name, not the picture, and the forgery has simply exposed the fact. There is truth here, since much of the fall in price reflects nothing loftier than the loss of a signature that could be resold. But the explanation proves too much; it implies that anyone who minds about the difference is a snob, including the scrupulous historian with no money at stake. The second says that the forgery must differ visibly after all, and that trained eyes, once alerted, can see its deadness. Sometimes this is so; yet the deadness is usually perceived only after the verdict is known, and a theory that can detect a difference only once it has been told where to look is not much of a theory.

A more promising account begins from the thought that we value paintings not only as arrangements of colour but also as achievements. To admire a picture fully is partly to admire what was done in making it: a problem of light or space confronted at a particular moment, with the means then available, by someone who did not know how it would turn out. The forger faces a different problem, that of producing something that will pass as the solution to the first. The two canvases may look alike, but they answer different questions, and the exposure tells us that the question we thought we were admiring an answer to was never asked by this canvas at all.

This view has a cost, and it should be admitted. It makes part of a painting's value depend on facts that cannot be seen in it, and so concedes that looking alone can never be the whole of appreciation. It also allows that a forgery may be a considerable achievement of its own kind, as a feat of imitation, without ranking it beside what it imitates. But the cost seems worth paying, because the alternative is to hold that the history of art could be rewritten, without loss, by anyone with a sufficiently skilful hand.

passage: The usual history of artificial light is a history of liberation. For most of human existence the coming of darkness set a hard limit on what people could do: work stopped, travel became dangerous, and the town shrank to the circle of the hearth. Oil lamps, then gas, then electricity pushed that limit back, until the night became little more than a dimmer continuation of the day, available for labour, commerce and pleasure. The story is not false. But it treats the night as an absence, a gap waiting to be filled, and in doing so it forgets that the pre-industrial night was a time with its own rules, its own inhabitants and its own uses.

In many European towns before public lighting, the night was governed differently from the day. Gates were shut, curfew bells were rung, and anyone abroad after dark without a lantern and a good reason might be stopped and questioned by the watch. The respectable stayed indoors; the streets belonged to watchmen, to those whose trades required darkness, to lovers, thieves and the young. This was not freedom in any simple sense, for the dark was also where violence went unpunished. It was, however, a separate jurisdiction, a time in which the authority of the day ran only weakly and in which much that could not be done openly was done.

The first systematic street lighting was installed less to lengthen the working day than to bring this jurisdiction under control. Its sponsors spoke of safety, and they meant it, but safety meant visibility, and visibility meant that the street at midnight could be watched and policed by the same standards as the street at noon. Accounts from several cities describe crowds breaking lamps in moments of unrest, and it is tempting to dismiss this as mere vandalism. It is more plausibly read as a recognition, however inarticulate, that the lamps were an extension of an authority that the crowd had reason to resist. The lamp, in this sense, was an instrument of the day carried into the night.

Yet to replace the story of liberation with a story of discipline would be to make the opposite mistake. Lighting did extend surveillance, but it also opened the night to people who had been effectively shut out of it. Respectable women, families, the elderly and the cautious could now walk to a theatre or a shop after dark, and whole new forms of sociability, from evening promenades to late markets, grew up in the lit streets. For many people the expansion of the policed night was, quite simply, an expansion of their world. The same lamp that exposed the thief to the watch made the street usable for the seamstress walking home.

What lighting did, then, was neither simply to free the night nor simply to conquer it, but to abolish it as a distinct social time. The day's rules, the day's people and the day's activities spread into hours that had once belonged to others. Those who had held the dark, the watchmen, the night trades and the young, lost not their lives but their hours, and the newcomers to the lit street rarely noticed what had been displaced. Whether we count this as a gain or a loss depends largely on whom we imagine walking the street, and it is precisely the habit of imagining only one kind of walker that has made the history of light so easy to tell and so hard to tell well.

passage: Discussions of antibiotic resistance usually begin with misuse: drugs prescribed for viral infections that they cannot touch, courses abandoned halfway, animals dosed to make them grow faster. Each of these practices gives bacteria more opportunities to evolve defences, and each deserves the attention it receives. Less often discussed is a quieter problem that has nothing to do with carelessness. Even if every prescription were perfectly judged, the way new antibiotics are paid for would discourage anyone from making them.

Consider what responsible use of a genuinely new antibiotic would look like. Because every use exerts selective pressure, the new drug should be held back for patients whose infections resist older and cheaper treatments, and it should be prescribed as rarely as possible for as long as possible. This is sound medicine. It is also a commercial disaster. A company recovers the cost of developing a drug by selling it in quantity during the years its patent protects it, and a drug that doctors are urged not to use cannot be sold in quantity. The contrast with a medicine for a chronic condition, taken every day for decades by millions of people, could hardly be sharper. It is not surprising that large firms have drifted out of the field, or that small firms that have brought new antibiotics through approval have sometimes failed commercially soon afterwards.

The proposed remedy is to separate a company's income from the number of doses it sells. Under such schemes, a health system would pay a fixed annual sum for access to a new antibiotic, whether it is used on a thousand patients or on ten, much as a town pays for a fire brigade whether or not anything burns that year. The payment rewards the existence of the drug rather than its consumption, which is exactly the property a reserve antibiotic is supposed to have.

The objections are real. Such payments are large, they must be justified to budget holders who see little use for their money, and nobody knows quite how to price a drug whose value lies mainly in emergencies it may never have to meet. Nor would better payment by itself guarantee discovery, since finding compounds that kill resistant bacteria without harming patients is scientifically hard. But these difficulties argue for designing the schemes carefully, not for abandoning them. The alternative is to go on rewarding a pattern of sales that good medicine forbids, and to discover the cost only when the older drugs have stopped working.

passage: It is often said that a scientific theory can never be proved but can always be refuted: no number of successful predictions establishes it, while a single failed one brings it down. The slogan captures something real about the asymmetry between confirmation and refutation, but as a description of how theories should be treated it is too simple. A prediction is never derived from a theory alone. It depends also on assumptions about the instruments used, the conditions of the experiment and the other bodies or forces that might be at work. When a prediction fails, logic tells us that something in this whole bundle is wrong; it does not tell us which part.

The history of astronomy offers a well-known illustration. In the first half of the nineteenth century, the observed orbit of Uranus departed from what Newtonian mechanics predicted. Astronomers did not abandon Newton. They supposed instead that an unseen planet was pulling on Uranus, calculated where it would have to be, and in 1846 Neptune was found close to the predicted position. The anomaly, far from refuting the theory, became one of its most celebrated successes.

The same strategy, however, does not always succeed. A small discrepancy in the orbit of Mercury was also attributed to an undiscovered planet, which some astronomers even named, but no such planet was ever found. The discrepancy was finally accounted for only by Einstein's general theory of relativity, which replaced Newton's account of gravitation rather than adding to it. In hindsight, the two anomalies look entirely different. At the time, they looked much the same, and the decision to treat both in the same way was reasonable.

The lesson is not that anomalies should be ignored, nor that theories should be given up at the first sign of trouble. It is that there is no rule which tells us in advance when an anomaly is a puzzle to be solved within a theory and when it is a sign that the theory is failing. Tenacity is a virtue in science, since a theory abandoned at the first difficulty would never have the chance to show what it can do; but tenacity shades into dogma when a theory is protected by one convenient assumption after another, each invented for no reason except to save it. Telling the two apart is a matter of judgement, informed by how many anomalies have accumulated and by whether the assumptions used to explain them away have earned independent support.

options.A: the theory must be replaced by another one that also explains its earlier successes.

options.D: at least one element of the theory and its accompanying assumptions is mistaken, though not which one.

passage: Two accounts of the professions have long competed for our assent, and each is right about something. The first, which professionals themselves favour, holds that a profession is defined by esoteric knowledge put at the service of clients who cannot judge it. Because a patient cannot assess a diagnosis or a litigant a legal argument, the state licenses practitioners, and the licence is a guarantee of competence that protects the public from charlatans. The second account, favoured by economists of a sceptical turn, treats the same licence as a barrier to entry: by limiting the number who may practise, a profession raises its fees, and its talk of public protection is simply the language in which a cartel describes itself.

What the two accounts share is more interesting than what divides them. Both look at one profession at a time, as if each stood alone facing its clients, and both assume that the work a profession does is simply given: there are diseases, so there are doctors; there are disputes, so there are lawyers. Yet the boundaries of professional work are anything but given. Whether persistent unhappiness is a medical condition, a psychological difficulty, a spiritual crisis or a social problem is not settled by the nature of unhappiness. It is settled, provisionally and repeatedly, by contests among psychiatrists, psychologists, clergy and social workers, each of whom claims that the problem properly belongs to it.

Seen from this angle, a profession is less a guild guarding a fixed territory than one party in a system of rival claims, and its history is a history of conquests and retreats. Licensing remains important, but as a weapon in a jurisdictional struggle rather than as either a certificate or a mere device for fixing prices. Knowledge, too, matters in a different way. What wins a contested problem is often not superior skill in treating it but a more abstract body of theory, one that allows a profession to redefine the problem in its own terms and so to argue that its rivals were treating the symptoms rather than the thing itself. A profession whose knowledge is purely practical can be displaced by one that can explain why that practice works.

This does not mean that competence is irrelevant or that the cartel theorist is merely cynical. Clients are protected by licensing, and fees are raised by it. But neither effect explains why some professions grow while others shrink, or why a body of practitioners who are perfectly good at their work can find that work quietly reassigned to others. The fate of a profession, on this view, depends less on how well it does what it does than on its ability to persuade others, including the state and the public, that the problems of the moment are its problems.

passage: Before the railways, every town kept its own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest over the local meridian, and because the sun appears to move westward, a town some distance to the west of another reached its noon a few minutes later. Nobody minded, because nothing travelled fast enough for the difference to matter; a coach journey of several days absorbed a quarter of an hour's discrepancy without anyone noticing it. The railway changed this, and the standard account of what followed is a story of practical necessity. Timetables drawn up in dozens of local times produced confusion and, on single-track lines, danger, so the companies adopted a single reference time and governments eventually followed.

The account is true as far as it goes, but it treats the change as a technical adjustment, like agreeing on a common gauge for the rails. It was more than that. Local time had been public in a literal sense: anyone could see the sun, and the clock on the church or the town hall was set by an observation that a curious citizen could, in principle, check. Standard time was set somewhere else, by astronomers in a distant observatory, and reached the town along a telegraph wire. The hour on the station clock was no longer a fact about the place where one stood but a decision taken elsewhere and transmitted to it.

This helps to explain a resistance that is usually remembered only as quaint. Some towns kept two clocks running side by side, or fitted a public dial with an extra hand so that the sun's reckoning and the railway's could be read together, and some local worthies denounced the new hour as an imposition. It is easy to read them as people clinging to habit in the face of progress. But they had grasped something that the language of convenience obscures: a shared standard is also a centre of authority, and agreeing to it means accepting that the definition of an everyday reality will henceforth be made by people one will never meet.

None of this is a case against standard time, whose benefits were real and soon taken for granted. Few people today would wish to return to a world in which the hour changed as one rode across a county. The argument is rather that the history of timekeeping is also a history of who is entitled to say what time it is, and that this question did not disappear when it was settled. Each later standard, from time signals broadcast by radio to the clocks that now synchronise themselves silently over networks, has extended the same arrangement, and each has made it a little harder to notice.

passage: Students and teachers share a reasonable-sounding rule: if learning feels smooth, it is going well. A chapter reread the night before an examination seems familiar, a set of problems practised one type at a time feels increasingly easy, and the growing ease is taken as proof of mastery. The rule is reasonable because in many activities fluency really does track competence. A pianist who plays a passage without stumbling has, in some sense, learned it. Yet in the specific matter of building knowledge that lasts and transfers, the rule is frequently misleading, and sometimes backwards.

The reason is that the conditions which make performance easy during study are often not the conditions which make memory durable. Rereading produces familiarity, the sense of having seen something before, which is easily mistaken for the ability to recall it unaided. Practising one kind of problem in a block lets the learner apply the same procedure again and again without ever deciding which procedure the problem calls for, the very decision a mixed examination demands. By contrast, spacing study sessions apart, testing oneself instead of rereading, and mixing problem types all make study feel slower and more error-prone, and all tend to produce better retention weeks later. The effort of retrieving a half-forgotten fact, or of working out which method applies, appears to be part of what fixes it in memory.

It would be easy to draw the wrong lesson from this, namely that harder is always better. It is not. A difficulty helps only when the learner can, with effort, overcome it; material pitched far beyond a student's grasp produces confusion rather than consolidation, and a test on something never learned teaches little except discouragement. The useful difficulties are those that call on processes the learner will later need, such as retrieval, discrimination and reconstruction, rather than obstacles that merely slow things down. Printing a textbook in a faint, awkward typeface makes reading harder, but there is little reason to expect it to make anything stick.

The deeper problem is one of judgement. Because learners rely on how study feels, they systematically prefer the methods that serve them worst, and they are not foolish to do so: the costs of effortful methods are felt now, while their benefits arrive later and unannounced. Teachers face a similar temptation, since a lesson in which students struggle looks, to an observer and to the students themselves, like a lesson that has gone badly. Changing practice therefore requires more than information about which methods work. It requires a willingness to distrust a feeling that is usually reliable, in exactly the setting where it is not.

passage: Few health instructions are repeated as confidently as the one about sleep: adults need about eight hours, and those hours should come in a single unbroken block. Someone who wakes at three in the morning and lies awake for an hour is likely to describe the experience as a disorder, and to spend the next day worrying about it. Advice is sought, remedies are bought, and an hour of wakefulness becomes a problem to be solved. Yet the second half of that instruction, the part about continuity, has a shorter history than its confidence suggests.

Historians reading diaries, legal testimony and household advice from pre-industrial Europe have noticed casual references to a 'first sleep' and a 'second sleep', separated by a spell of wakefulness in the middle of the night. People used that interval to pray, tend the fire, talk quietly, or simply lie in the dark and think. What is striking about these references is not their content but their tone: the waking interval is mentioned as an ordinary feature of the night, not as a complaint. One explanation offered for its later disappearance is the spread of cheap artificial light, which pushed bedtimes later and compressed the night into a single shorter stretch, though the evidence for this is suggestive rather than conclusive.

If consolidated sleep is partly a product of custom, then some of what is now labelled insomnia may be a mismatch between a person and a norm rather than a fault in the person. This matters because worry about sleep is itself a powerful disrupter of sleep. A person who wakes in the night and concludes that something has gone wrong becomes more alert, and stays awake longer, than one who regards the waking as unremarkable. The norm, in other words, can help produce the very failures it is used to diagnose.

It would be a mistake, however, to replace one myth with another. The historical record does not show that segmented sleep is the true human pattern from which industrial society has led us astray; it shows that sleep has taken more than one form, depending on light, work and season. Nor does any of this make chronic sleep loss harmless. People who sleep too little over long periods do suffer for it, and some sleep complaints call for medical attention. The modest lesson is that a description of how many people sleep should not be mistaken for a rule about how everyone must.

passage: Discussions of the so-called file drawer problem usually begin with journals. Editors, the complaint runs, prefer results that show something: a drug that works, an effect that appears, a difference between groups. Studies that find nothing are harder to place, and so they remain in researchers' filing cabinets while the published literature fills up with positive findings. A reader who surveys that literature will then overestimate how often, and how strongly, the effect in question occurs, since the failures that would have tempered the estimate never reached print. The literature, in other words, is not a sample of the research that was done but a selection from it, made on the very quantity that readers most want to estimate.

There is truth in this account, and the remedy it suggests, journals that commit in advance to publishing well-conducted studies whatever they find, deserves the support it has received. But the account places the drawer in the wrong office. Ask a working scientist what became of her last inconclusive experiment and the answer is seldom that an editor turned it down. More often it was never written up at all. The study was abandoned before any journal had a chance to reject it, and it sits in the drawer because its own author put it there.

The reason is not laziness. A positive result, whatever its other defects, announces itself: something happened. A null result is mute about its own meaning. It may show that the effect does not exist, or that the sample was too small to detect it, or that a reagent was contaminated, or that a student misread the protocol. The researcher who obtained it is often the person least able to tell which, and the most honest description she could offer, that she looked and did not see, is one that few colleagues would think worth the trouble of reading. Writing such a paper costs weeks and earns little, and the decision to move on is, from where she stands, entirely rational.

If this is right, obliging journals to accept null results treats the symptom at the far end. The drawer will empty only when null results become informative, and that depends on decisions made before any data are collected: samples large enough that a real effect would probably have been seen, procedures specified in advance so that a failure cannot be blamed afterwards on improvisation, checks built in to show that the apparatus was working. A null result obtained under such conditions says something definite, and researchers will publish it for the same reason they publish anything, because it tells their colleagues something they did not know.

passage: Insurance works by pooling: many people each pay a modest premium so that the few who suffer a loss can be compensated, and the arrangement rests on a fact that is easy to overlook: no one in the pool knows in advance who the unlucky will be. If the pool holds a mixture of people whose risks differ but cannot be told apart, a single price can cover everyone, and the careful and the careless alike buy protection they value.

The trouble begins when buyers know more about their own risk than the insurer does. Those who expect to claim find a uniform premium a bargain; those who expect not to find it expensive, and some of them leave. The insurer, seeing claims rise relative to premiums, raises the price, which drives out the next group of relatively safe customers. In the extreme case the pool shrinks until only the riskiest remain, and a product that many people would have wanted cannot be sold at a price that anyone else will pay. Economists call this unravelling adverse selection, and it can happen even though no one has lied to anyone.

Two remedies are available, and neither is free. The first is for insurers to close the gap in information through medical examinations, questionnaires and records of past claims. Each of these helps, yet each also wears away the pooling that made insurance worth having, because a pool sorted precisely by risk is no longer sharing much risk at all. A person found to have a costly condition before buying cover will be quoted a premium close to the expected cost of treating it, which is to say no insurance in any useful sense. The second remedy is to make membership compulsory or nearly universal, so that the low-risk cannot walk away. This keeps the pool mixed, but it asks the healthy to subsidise the sick on terms that some of them did not choose and regard as unfair.

The choice between these remedies is often presented as a technical matter for actuaries, but it is better understood as a choice about how much of life's bad luck a society wishes to share. For risks that people largely take on by choice, such as a dangerous hobby, pricing by risk seems fair enough. For risks that arrive at birth or by pure chance, sorting begins to look like penalising people twice: once through fate, and again through the price.

passage: For a period, small loans to the poor were spoken of as something close to a cure. The story was compelling: a woman borrows a modest sum, buys a second sewing machine or a stock of vegetables to sell, repays from her profits, borrows again, and climbs by degrees out of poverty. Lenders who reported repayment rates that conventional banks could only envy seemed to prove that the poor were creditworthy, and from creditworthiness it seemed a short step to prosperity. The step proved longer than advertised.

When careful evaluations compared similar communities with and without access to microcredit, they tended to find effects that were real but modest. Some households started or expanded businesses; average incomes and consumption rose little, if at all; and the transformation of lives promised in the brochures was hard to find in the data. It would be easy to read this as a verdict that microcredit failed. That reading, I think, mistakes what was being tested. The original story assumed that most poor people are frustrated entrepreneurs held back only by a lack of capital. Many are not. They run tiny enterprises because steady wage work is unavailable, and given the choice many would take a factory job at a fixed wage over the uncertainties of a market stall.

Seen in this light, the more interesting finding is how borrowers actually used their loans. A good deal of the money went not into enterprises but into managing life's lumpy expenses: a wedding, a hospital bill, school fees due all at once, a new roof before the rains. For households whose incomes arrive irregularly, the ability to turn a stream of small repayments into a single usable sum is genuinely valuable, even if it never shows up as a rise in average income. Microcredit, on this view, is less an engine of growth than a financial service, comparable to the savings and insurance that the better-off take for granted.

This reframing is not a licence for complacency. Where lenders multiply and compete for the same clients, households can take one loan to repay another, and a service that smooths hardship can become a source of it. Nor should the modest average conceal a minority of borrowers, usually those who already ran established businesses, for whom credit made a larger difference. The lesson is not that small loans are worthless but that they should be judged as what they are, and regulated with that in mind, rather than against a promise they were never likely to keep.

passage: For a time it seemed that psychology had found the mechanism of willpower. Self-control, the theory held, draws on a limited resource that is used up by effort and replenished by rest. Resisting a tempting food, suppressing an emotion or forcing oneself through a tedious task would each deplete the same store, leaving a person less able to exercise control on whatever came next. The idea had the great advantage of matching experience. Most of us know the evening collapse that follows a day of holding ourselves together, and the theory seemed to explain it with all the economy of a fuel gauge. It also seemed to account for a scattering of everyday puzzles: why a dieter might lapse late in the day rather than at breakfast, why hard decisions get put off until morning, why a quarrel flares more easily after a draining afternoon.

The theory has fared badly under closer scrutiny. Large coordinated attempts to reproduce the basic effect, in which many laboratories ran the same procedure, found it to be far smaller than early reports had suggested and in some cases close to nothing. A particularly vivid version of the theory, which identified the resource with blood sugar and held that a sweet drink could restore flagging self-control, met an additional difficulty: effortful thinking appears to change the brain's overall energy consumption only slightly, far too little for the proposed mechanism to work as described. Some studies also reported that people who believed willpower to be plentiful showed little or no depletion, a result awkward for any theory in which the resource is a physical quantity.

Yet it does not follow that the experience the theory set out to explain is an illusion. People do grow less willing to persist after sustained effort, and that change deserves an account. A more promising one treats the feeling of mental fatigue not as a reading on an emptying tank but as a signal about priorities. On this view, continued effort on one task carries an opportunity cost, the value of everything else one might be doing instead, and the sense of weariness rises as that cost accumulates, nudging attention away from obligation and towards rest, pleasure or novelty. What looks like running out is better described as a shift in what the mind is willing to pay for.

The difference between the two pictures is not merely academic. If willpower is a fuel, the sensible strategy is rationing: avoid unnecessary decisions, save strength for what matters, and accept failure when the tank is low. If fatigue is a signal about value, the strategy changes. Tasks that feel meaningful or rewarding should be less draining than equally demanding tasks that do not, and changing how a task is framed, or what it leads to, may restore persistence where rest alone would not. The second picture does not make self-control easy, but it relocates the problem from the size of a store to the weighing of competing goods. It also suggests why the same evening can feel exhausting at a desk and effortless at a hobby, though the demands on attention may be much the same.

The episode also carries a lesson about how attractive ideas spread. The resource model was simple, intuitive and flattering to common experience, and these virtues helped it travel far beyond the evidence that supported it. None of this required anyone to be careless or dishonest; it is simply how persuasive ideas tend to behave. Its decline is not a refutation of everyday wisdom about tiredness; it is a reminder that a vivid metaphor can capture a real phenomenon while getting its mechanism entirely wrong.

passage: Most moral theories divide actions into three kinds: those we are required to do, those we are forbidden to do, and those that are merely permitted, yet ordinary moral thought seems to need a fourth. When a passer-by plunges into a freezing river to rescue a stranger, we do not say that she merely did something permitted, as though her act ranked alongside choosing tea over coffee. Nor do we say that she did her duty, for we would not have condemned her had she stayed on the riverbank and called for help. We say instead that she went beyond what duty asked. Acts of this kind are called supererogatory, and their existence has proved surprisingly awkward for theories that try to derive the whole of morality from a single principle.

The difficulty is sharpest for a simple form of consequentialism, the view that we are always required to do whatever produces the best outcome. On that view there is no room above duty, because the best available act is always the required one. If plunging into the river was the best thing she could do, she was obliged to do it; if it was not, she acted wrongly. Heroism disappears into ordinary obligation, and the person who fails to be a hero becomes a wrongdoer. Many critics take this to be a decisive objection: a theory that makes sainthood compulsory has misunderstood what morality is for.

Defenders reply that the objection confuses two questions: what one ought to do and what one may be blamed for not doing. Perhaps we should not blame the bystander who stays on the riverbank, since blaming people for failing to be heroes would be useless or cruel, while still holding that the rescue was what she ought to have done. This move is ingenious, and it does capture something; our reluctance to blame is partly practical. But it leaves the rescuer's own understanding of her act unexplained, for people who perform such acts often say, sincerely, that they had no choice, yet they rarely say that those who held back did wrong. Their sense of being called is personal, not a verdict on everyone.

What this suggests is that the space beyond duty is real but has a peculiar shape. It is not a zone of optional extras to which morality is indifferent, since such acts are admired precisely as moral achievements. Nor is it simply duty under a gentler name. It is the region where morality stops issuing demands to everyone and starts issuing invitations to particular people, and a theory that can speak only in demands will always misdescribe it.

passage: Among professional historians it has become something of a reflex to sneer at heritage. The restored cottage with its costumed guide, the festival that re-enacts a battle every summer, the gift shop selling replica coins and the television drama in which everyone has perfect teeth are all, on this view, so many falsifications: a past made comfortable, sold by the ticket and stripped of everything that might disturb a family on a day out. The critics are not wrong about the facts. Heritage does select, simplify and flatter, and it usually offers the past with the smell taken out.

What the critique misses is that heritage is not attempting to be history and failing at it. The two draw on the same materials, the same buildings, objects and stories, but they put them to different uses. History asks questions of the past and follows the evidence wherever it leads, including towards conclusions that unsettle the people who hear them. Heritage asks the past to confirm something about the present: that this town has deep roots, that this people has endured, that the place where one lives is worth caring about. Its characteristic question is not 'what happened here, and why?' but 'why should this place and its people matter to us?', and its characteristic answer is an experience rather than an argument. It is closer to commemoration than to inquiry, and it should be judged as commemoration is judged.

Consider a family that marks a grandparent's long marriage with a party, old photographs on the walls and affectionate speeches. Nobody expects the speeches to include an account of the couple's worst quarrels, and nobody thinks the omission a lie; the occasion exists to celebrate, and everyone present understands this. The tidying that heritage performs is, in the same way, not itself the offence. A restored village that shows thatched roofs and spinning wheels but not the open drains or the cramped rooms where servants slept is doing what celebrations do. There is even a case that it does history a service, for many people first sense that the past was inhabited by real people when they stand in such a room, and the curiosity awakened there leads some of them on to the harder questions that history asks.

The trouble begins at a specific point, and it is worth locating precisely. It comes when heritage claims the authority of history: when a site presents its selective story not as a celebration but as an account of how things really were, when a guidebook dismisses awkward evidence as the invention of cynics, or when public money that once sustained archives and libraries is redirected to attractions that will draw larger crowds. A museum label that calls a disputed episode 'settled', or a re-enactment whose script quietly drops the side that lost, does more than simplify; it borrows the standing of scholarship in order to close a question that scholarship has left open. At that point celebration has stopped being one use of the past among others and has begun to crowd out the use that tests it.

The sensible relation between the two is neither contempt nor merger. History should remain the critic of heritage, ready to point out what a display leaves out and to say so in public; heritage can remain what it is, a doorway through which many people first enter the past. The line that needs defending is not the one between the professional and the popular, but the one between celebration that knows itself to be celebration and celebration that presents itself as knowledge.

passage: It is natural to think of understanding as knowledge in a higher concentration. On this view, a person who understands why bridges stand or why prices rise simply knows more than one who does not: more facts, and in particular more facts about causes. Understanding would then be knowledge of a special subject matter, the reasons why, but it would be knowledge all the same, answerable to the same standards and vulnerable to the same defeats.

The view has difficulty with a familiar figure, the student who has memorised the correct explanation. Asked why the seasons change, she replies, accurately, that the earth's axis is tilted relative to the plane of its orbit, so that each hemisphere receives more direct sunlight for part of the year. She has the answer from a reliable textbook and a reliable teacher, and by most accounts of knowledge she knows why the seasons change. Yet ask her what would happen if the tilt were greater, or why the seasons are reversed between the hemispheres, and she is at a loss. She possesses the explanation as a sentence rather than as something she can use. What she lacks is not a further fact but a grasp of how the facts she already has depend on one another, the ability to follow the explanation into cases for which it was not stated.

If this is right, understanding is less a matter of what one has been told than of what one can do with it, and this has a surprising consequence. Knowledge is usually held to require truth: one cannot know what is false. Understanding seems more forgiving. Much of what we rightly call scientific understanding is achieved through models that are, taken literally, false. The simple model of a gas treats its molecules as points that occupy no space and exert no forces on one another except in collision, which no actual molecule does; yet a student who has mastered that model understands a great deal about why gases behave as they do, and understands it partly because the model leaves out complications that would obscure the pattern. It would be odd to say that her understanding is defective merely because the model is false, and odder still to say that someone who had memorised a more accurate description, but could do nothing with it, understood more.

This should not be taken to mean that understanding floats free of truth altogether. An idealisation earns its place only when its departures from reality are irrelevant to the questions it is used to answer; the point-particle model serves well for gases at ordinary densities and misleads at very high ones, and part of understanding the model is knowing where it stops working. A story that got the dependencies wrong, however fluently it could be manipulated, would yield not understanding but a skilful illusion of it. The claim, then, is not that falsehood is harmless but that the relation between understanding and truth is looser and more selective than the relation between knowledge and truth: understanding demands accuracy in the respects that bear on the dependencies grasped, and tolerates distortion elsewhere.

The distinction matters beyond philosophy. Educational systems that measure success by the reproduction of correct statements will reward the memorising student and may never detect what she is missing, since what she is missing shows itself only when the question changes. Testing for understanding requires, at least in part, asking questions the student has not been prepared for.

passage: For a long time the sociology of taste worked with a simple map. At the top of the social order sat a refined culture of opera, poetry and the old masters, at the bottom sat popular entertainments, and a person's place in society could be read, with fair accuracy, from the position of their preferences on this ladder. Elites, on this picture, distinguished themselves by what they refused. Liking the wrong music was not merely a private failing but a mark of origin.

Surveys of cultural consumption in a number of wealthy countries have since complicated the map. The most educated and affluent groups, it turns out, are no longer best described as snobs who like only high culture. They are more often omnivores: they go to the opera and to the cinema, read literary fiction and crime novels, and are happy to discuss both a string quartet and a pop album. Some observers have greeted this as the end of cultural hierarchy, a sign that the old boundaries between high and low have dissolved and that taste has become a matter of individual preference rather than of class.

That conclusion is premature. Breadth of taste is itself unevenly distributed, because it requires money, time, travel and, above all, the confidence to move between worlds without feeling out of place. The person who can talk knowledgeably about both a symphony and a street-food stall has accumulated a cultural range that is far harder to acquire than a liking for either alone. Moreover, omnivores rarely consume popular forms in the same way as their usual audiences. They tend to approach them with a knowing, curatorial attitude, prizing a song for its place in the history of a genre or enjoying a film with a touch of irony, and this manner of liking can mark distance as effectively as refusal once did.

Nor is the omnivore's appetite unlimited. Research on what people say they dislike has suggested that the forms most often rejected by the highly educated tend to be those most associated with the least educated, so that the boundary has moved rather than vanished. None of this means that the loosening of old hierarchies is an illusion; it is a genuine change that the opera house must now compete for prestige with a well-chosen food truck. But distinction has not disappeared with the decline of snobbery. It has learned to express itself through openness, and openness is harder to criticise than exclusion because it looks so much like a virtue.

passage: When two researchers, one celebrated and one unknown, publish a discovery together, the discovery is very likely to be remembered as the celebrated researcher's. The same pattern appears when two people arrive at a result independently: the one who is already eminent tends to receive the larger share of the attention, the citations and the invitations that follow. Sociologists of science named this the Matthew effect, after the verse in the Gospel of Matthew about those who have being given more, and it is usually discussed as a problem of fairness. The unknown co-author did much of the work, and someone else collected the credit.

That description is correct within its limits, but it understates what is at stake, and it also misses why the effect is so persistent. Scientists face a literature far larger than anyone could read in a lifetime. A familiar name on a paper is a cheap signal that the paper is probably worth the reader's time, and in a world of scarce attention, readers who rely on such signals are not being foolish. To some degree, then, the effect is the by-product of a reasonable strategy for coping with abundance. Condemning it as mere snobbery does not explain why careful and fair-minded people take part in it every day.

The trouble begins when attention is converted into resources. A researcher whose papers are widely read finds it easier to win grants, which pay for students and equipment, which produce more papers, which are read more widely still. Advantage compounds. After a few rounds, the difference between two careers may bear little relation to any difference in the quality of their first ideas, and the field as a whole has placed a heavy bet on one line of work for reasons that are partly accidental. Ideas that happened to originate with the less visible researcher may wait years for a hearing, or never receive one, not because they were tested and found wanting but because nobody with the means to test them was looking in their direction.

Seen in this light, the effect is less an injustice done to individuals than a distortion in how a field allocates its bets, and the remedy is not to forbid readers from noticing names, which would be both futile and costly. It is to loosen the link between attention and money: to judge some grant proposals without knowing who wrote them, to set aside funds for researchers early in their careers, and to treat a famous name as a reason to read a paper rather than as a reason to believe it.

passage: It has become common to say that colonial censuses did not so much count the peoples of the empire as invent them. The enumerator arrived with a schedule of questions and a list of permitted answers, and the population that emerged from the tables, divided into neatly bounded communities of religion, caste, tribe and language, was in this view largely a creation of the administrative imagination. The argument has done valuable work. It has made historians suspicious of treating census categories as simple descriptions of a pre-existing social order, and it has drawn attention to the way in which knowledge and rule were bound together. Yet in its strongest form it claims too much, and in claiming too much it obscures what was genuinely new.

The distinctions that census officials recorded were not conjured out of nothing. People in the societies being counted had long spoken of lineage, occupation, locality, sect and status, and had used these terms to arrange marriages, settle disputes and decide whom to eat with. What these older vocabularies did not usually require was that a person belong to exactly one category of each kind, at all times and for all purposes. A weaver might describe himself by his craft in the market, by his lineage at a wedding and by his village when travelling, without feeling that any one of these was his real identity. The census demanded a single answer, written once and then aggregated, and it treated a blank or a double answer as an error to be corrected.

The novelty, then, lay less in the categories than in what was done with them. Once fixed and counted, a category could be ranked, compared across districts, and used as the basis for decisions about recruitment, land and, later, political representation. Groups discovered that their recorded size and standing had consequences, and petitions asking to be listed under a different name or placed higher in an official order of precedence became a regular feature of census years. Some observers have treated such petitions as proof that the categories were artificial, mere labels that people manipulated for advantage. But the petitions suggest the opposite conclusion. People do not campaign over labels that mean nothing to them; they campaign over labels that have begun to govern their lives.

This is why the categories outlived the governments that produced them. An identity that is only imposed can be thrown off when its author departs. An identity that has been taken up, argued over and attached to rights and resources becomes part of the social world it was once supposed merely to describe. The census, in short, was neither a mirror nor a fiction. It was closer to a mould, into which existing and quite fluid materials were pressed until they set.

passage: Income is the most convenient measure of how well people are doing, and convenience has a way of turning into authority. A figure for income per head can be compared across countries and decades, added up and divided, and reported to a decimal place. Yet what it measures is a means. People do not value income for its own sake but for what it allows them to do and to be: to be adequately nourished, to move about without danger, to read, to take part in the life of a community, to have some say in the decisions that shape their lives. The capability approach, as it has come to be called, proposes that development should be judged by these freedoms directly rather than by the resources that are supposed to produce them.

The case for the shift rests on a simple observation with large consequences. The same income does not yield the same freedoms to everyone. A person who uses a wheelchair needs more resources than a neighbour to reach the same workplace; a pregnant woman needs more food than a man of the same age to be equally well nourished; a household in a cold climate must spend on heating what a household elsewhere can spend on anything it likes. Social arrangements matter as much as bodies and climates. Where custom keeps women from travelling alone, a rise in household income may leave a daughter's freedom to attend a distant college exactly where it was. Measures of income, by construction, are blind to these differences in the rate at which resources become lives.

The standard objection is that the approach, whatever its philosophical appeal, cannot be made to work. Which capabilities count? How should being literate be weighed against being healthy, or political voice against freedom from hunger? Any answer, critics say, is either so vague as to be useless or, once written down as a definite list with definite weights, an imposition of some theorist's values on people who might rank their lives differently. A list drawn up in a university, they add, need not be the list that a farmer or a factory worker would draw up, and a framework that began by taking people's own lives seriously would then end by overruling their judgments about those lives.

The objection is weaker than it looks, because it applies with equal force to the measure it is meant to defend. Income per head also aggregates very different things, and it also weights them. It weights them by market prices, which record what people with money are willing to pay, so that a luxury bought by the rich can count for more than a staple that the poor cannot afford. These are value judgments as well; they are simply made silently, by the market, rather than openly, by someone who must defend them. A framework that forces its users to state and argue for their weights has not introduced a new difficulty. It has exposed an old one.

This does not mean that every attempt to turn capabilities into a single index succeeds. Composite scores that average a few indicators can reproduce the very problem the approach set out to solve, burying under one number the differences in conversion that made income misleading in the first place. The approach is at its strongest not as a rival ranking but as a discipline of attention: a way of asking, in any given place, which freedoms people lack and why, and of noticing when a rising average conceals a stagnant life.

passage: A randomised trial, for all its authority, answers a question about groups. It tells us that among patients like those enrolled, the people given a treatment did better on average than the people who were not, by an amount that can be estimated with known uncertainty. The doctor in a consulting room faces a different question, about a single person, and the gap between the two questions has produced two opposite errors, each of which presents itself as wisdom.

The first error is to apply the average as though it were a fact about each patient. If a drug lowers the risk of a stroke over five years from ten in a hundred to seven in a hundred, it is tempting to say that it reduces every patient's risk by three points. But the trial cannot show this. The same average would result if a small minority benefited a great deal and everyone else not at all, or if many benefited modestly while a few were harmed. An average is a summary of a distribution, and very different distributions share the same summary. Even afterwards the matter stays hidden: a patient who takes the drug and has no stroke cannot tell whether the drug or good fortune spared him. To promise a particular patient a reduction of three points is to claim knowledge the trial does not contain.

The second error starts from this observation and draws the wrong conclusion. Since every patient is different, it says, trial results do not apply to the person in front of me, and I must rely on my clinical judgement. The premise is true and the conclusion does not follow. That patients differ is not news; what matters is whether they differ in ways that change how they respond to this treatment, and the clinician's impression is a poor instrument for discovering that. A doctor's experience is itself a kind of trial, but one without randomisation, with a small sample, no comparison group and a memory that favours vivid cases. If a large trial cannot reveal who benefits, a recollection of a few dozen patients is unlikely to do better.

Nor is the obvious remedy, examining subgroups within the trial, as reliable as it appears. Divide a trial's patients by age, sex, severity and a dozen other features, and some subgroups will show striking benefit or none at all purely by chance; the more divisions are made, the more such mirages appear. Findings of this kind have often failed to reappear when tested again. This does not mean that genuine differences in response do not exist. It means that claims about them need evidence as demanding as the evidence for the average itself, such as a plausible mechanism together with a difference that recurs in a fresh trial.

What follows is neither the tyranny of the average nor the licence of intuition. The average is the best default available when nothing more is known, and departures from it should be justified by reasons rather than by a sense that this patient is special. For some chronic conditions whose symptoms come and go quickly, it is even possible to run a trial within a single patient, alternating the treatment with a placebo over several periods and comparing the results. Such designs are not always practical, but they show what an answer to the individual question would actually require, and how little the bare assertion of individuality provides.
